In the Nagpur flat, Sudha dragged her yellow blanket over to Sarika and held it up, eyes heavy. Sarika wrapped her in it and pulled her onto her lap.
Later Sudha's baby cousin woke from her nap wailing. Sudha slid off Sarika's lap, went to the cot, and patted the baby's leg, pat, pat, pat, just the way Sarika pats her.
“You're helping,” said Sarika, smiling. The baby kept crying, and Sudha looked back at her mother, unsure.

qa.q: What colour was Sudha's blanket?
qa.a: Her blanket was yellow.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she held up her blanket to Sarika?
qa.a: She was tired and wanted comfort; her heavy eyes and the blanket held out showed she wanted to be cuddled.

qa.q: How could Sarika help when Sudha looks back unsure?
qa.a: She could come over, pick up the baby, and show Sudha the next step, thanking her for trying.

qa.q: How did Sarika see Sudha's patting of the baby?
qa.a: Sarika seemed pleased and touched, seeing Sudha copy the way she comforts her, and said "You're helping."

grounding: It shows a toddler holding out her blanket to be comforted and patting a crying baby in imitation of the care she receives.

passage:
In the village courtyard, Ujjwal snatched the neighbour girl's clay whistle and ran. She burst into tears.
His aunt Bidisha caught up with him. “Ujjwal, she's crying. You took her whistle. Say sorry.”
Ujjwal looked at the whistle, then at the girl. He walked back, held it out at arm's length, and when she took it, he flung both arms round her in a clumsy hug.
“Sorry,” Bidisha said for him, softly. The girl sniffed, and blew the whistle.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal snatch from the neighbour girl?
qa.a: He snatched her clay whistle.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's clumsy hug suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he felt some unease at her tears and wanted to make things right; the hug is an early repair, prompted by his aunt, more than an understanding of fault.

qa.q: How did Bidisha help Ujjwal repair things?
qa.a: She named what happened simply, prompted him to give the whistle back, and said "sorry" for him to model the word.

qa.q: How might the neighbour girl feel after getting her whistle back with a hug?
qa.a: She is probably comforted and ready to play again, since she sniffed and blew the whistle.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler giving back a grabbed toy and hugging after an adult prompts sorry, showing early repair more than understanding of fault.

subtype: Likes and dislikes as strong assertions [Expressing]
passage:
At dinner in the Bhopal flat, Zeenat grabbed her red cup with both hands. “Mine!”
“Yes, your red cup,” said Papa, Pradeep.
He spooned dal onto her plate. She pushed the plate away. “No!”
He tried rice. She grabbed a handful and stuffed it in, humming.
“She's being difficult,” said Dadi.
“She knows what she likes,” said Pradeep, and left the dal at the side of her plate for later.

qa.q: What colour was Zeenat's cup?
qa.a: Her cup was red.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when she pushed away the dal and said "No!"?
qa.a: She was firm and a bit cross about food she didn't want, while her humming over the rice shows she was happy with what she liked; she was asserting her preferences more than being defiant.

qa.q: What did Pradeep do that respects Zeenat's growing independence?
qa.a: He named her cup as hers, didn't force the dal, and left it at the side of the plate for later.

qa.q: How does Dadi see Zeenat's refusals?
qa.a: Dadi sees them as being difficult.

grounding: It shows a toddler grabbing her cup and refusing food with mine and no, expressing preference and independence rather than defiance alone.

subtype: Toddler cries, points and single words [Expressing]
passage:
“Why is Kamal crying again?” asked Abbu.
“Let me check,” said Rehana. “Kamal, more?” She held up a biscuit. He pushed it away.
“Water?” He shook his head and cried harder.
“Sleepy?” He'd napped well. She felt his forehead. “Not hot.”
Kamal pointed down and wailed. “Owie!”
Rehana looked. His new sandal strap was pressing a red line into his foot.
“Oh, jaan! That hurts.” She unbuckled it, and the crying stopped.

qa.q: What was pressing a red line into Kamal's foot?
qa.a: His new sandal strap.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling as he pointed down and wailed?
qa.a: He was in pain from the tight strap, and frustrated that his crying wasn't understood at first.

qa.q: What did Rehana do that helped her find the cause?
qa.a: She checked food, drink, sleep and temperature in turn, and then followed Kamal's pointing to his foot.

qa.q: How did Abbu see Kamal's crying at first?
qa.a: Abbu seemed puzzled and a bit weary, asking why Kamal was crying again.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler signalling a need through crying, pushing away, pointing and a single word, with an adult checking possible needs in turn.

passage:
“Time to go home, Asif,” said Payal Aunty at the park gate.
“No! No!” Asif whined, and threw his ball into the bushes.
“He's being naughty,” said his sister Aliya.
Asif went floppy on the path, a heavy little sack.
Payal crouched. “You're cross. You wanted more slide. We're still going home.” She waited.
Asif grumbled into the dirt.
“Want to carry the ball or hold my hand?”
He sniffed, got up, and held out his hand.

qa.q: Where did Asif throw his ball?
qa.a: He threw his ball into the bushes.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he whined, threw the ball and went floppy?
qa.a: He was frustrated that his fun was ending and probably tired, rather than just being naughty.

qa.q: How did Payal Aunty handle Asif's protest well?
qa.a: She stayed calm, named the feeling, held the limit that they were going home, and offered a small choice.

qa.q: How does Aliya see Asif going floppy?
qa.a: Aliya sees it as naughtiness.

grounding: It shows a toddler whining, throwing and going limp in protest, and an adult setting a calm limit and naming the feeling.

passage:
In the Copenhagen daycare, Oliver took Daniel's yellow digger. Daniel's face went red. He leaned over and bit Oliver's arm.
Oliver howled. Ingrid, the teacher, was there in a second. She checked Oliver's arm first: red marks, no broken skin. Then she knelt by Daniel.
“You were angry. He took your digger. Biting hurts. You can stamp your feet and say ‘mine.’”
Daniel stamped hard. “Mine!”
Ingrid helped Oliver find another truck.

qa.q: What colour was Daniel's digger?
qa.a: Daniel's digger was yellow.

qa.q: What was Daniel feeling when he bit Oliver?
qa.a: He was angry and frustrated that his digger was taken, and without the words to say so, the feeling came out as a bite, not as malice.

qa.q: What did Ingrid do that a wise teacher would copy?
qa.a: She checked Oliver first, then named Daniel's anger, said biting hurts, and showed him a safer action, stamping and saying "mine."

qa.q: What was it like for Oliver when Daniel bit him?
qa.a: It hurt and frightened him, which is why he howled.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler biting when frustrated, signalling a strong feeling rather than malice, and an adult naming the feeling and showing a safer action.

passage:
“Amma! Owie!” Santosh held up his arm, showing a blue bruise above his elbow.
Manjula knelt and looked calmly. “I see it. What happened?”
“Scared,” he said, lip trembling. He pointed to the note in his bag.
Manjula read it: bumped on the climbing frame, cold cloth given. “You bumped at daycare, and it scared you.”
“Scared,” he said again, nodding.
“Thank you for showing Amma.” She kissed near the bruise. “Tell me anytime."

qa.q: Where was Santosh's bruise?
qa.a: The bruise was above his elbow.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when he showed Manjula the bruise?
qa.a: He was still a bit frightened by the bump, as his trembling lip and the word "Scared" show, and wanted his Amma to know.

qa.q: Why was Manjula's calm response a good one?
qa.a: She looked, asked, checked the daycare note, put the story into words and thanked him, which encourages Santosh to keep telling her things.

qa.q: What would change if Manjula had brushed it off with "It's nothing"?
qa.a: Santosh might feel his fear didn't matter and be less likely to show or tell her things later.

grounding: It shows a toddler showing a bruise and saying scared, a brief, concrete early disclosure, and a parent responding calmly to encourage confiding.

passage:
In a small kitchen in Sydney, Tuan's uncle Alejandro hid his face behind a tea towel. “Where's Tuan?” He pulled it down. “Boo!”
Tuan shrieked with laughter and slapped the table. “Again!”
Alejandro did it again, and again, and each time Tuan laughed just as hard, waiting with his mouth open for the “Boo!”
At the café later, a stranger tried peekaboo with a menu. Tuan stared, unsure, and leaned back into his uncle's chest.

qa.q: What did Alejandro hide his face behind?
qa.a: He hid his face behind a tea towel.

qa.q: What was Tuan feeling during peekaboo with his uncle, and why was it different with the stranger?
qa.a: With his uncle he was delighted, waiting for the "Boo!" he knew was coming; with the stranger he felt unsure and wary, because the game depends on a safe, familiar partner.

qa.q: What could the stranger have done instead?
qa.a: The stranger could have smiled from a distance and let Tuan get used to them before trying a surprise game.

qa.q: What is it like for Alejandro when Tuan shouts "Again!"?
qa.a: Alejandro probably feels delighted and close to Tuan, happy to repeat the game.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler laughing at peekaboo with a familiar uncle and repeating it, and the same game from a stranger making him wary.

passage:
In the Johannesburg flat, Zanele held a banana to her ear. “Hello! Hello, Gogo!”
Marek, her father, laughed. “Tell Gogo I said hi.”
Then he put on music. “Hop like a bunny!” Zanele hopped, giggling, hands up like ears.
Rain started hammering the window. “Wow, it's raining cats and dogs,” said Marek.
Zanele ran to the window and pressed her nose to the glass, searching. “Where doggy?”
Marek crouched beside her. “No doggies. Just lots of rain."

qa.q: What did Zanele hold to her ear as a phone?
qa.a: She held a banana to her ear.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling when she ran to the window looking for the dogs?
qa.a: She was excited and curious, taking the words literally and expecting to see real dogs, which shows the saying meant nothing to her yet.

qa.q: How did Marek respond well when Zanele took the idiom literally?
qa.a: He crouched beside her and explained simply, "No doggies. Just lots of rain," without laughing at her.

qa.q: How might Marek feel watching Zanele search the window?
qa.a: He would likely feel amused and tender, realising she heard his words exactly as spoken.

grounding: It shows a toddler treating a banana as a phone and enjoying hop like a bunny, while taking an idiom literally.

passage:
On Sunday evening in their London flat, Liam's grandmother bowed her head before dinner and folded her hands. Amara, his mother, did the same.
Liam watched, then pressed his own chubby hands together, squeezed his eyes shut and waited.
As soon as Granny said “Amen,” Liam shouted, “A-MEN!” and grabbed a potato.
Everyone laughed. Granny patted his head. “Good boy, joining in.”
Amara smiled. He didn't know what it meant yet, only that he belonged at that table.

qa.q: What did Liam grab after shouting "A-MEN"?
qa.a: He grabbed a potato.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling when he folded his hands and shouted "A-MEN!"?
qa.a: He was proud and happy to join in with his family, copying what they did, rather than expressing a belief he understood.

qa.q: How did the family respond in a way that supports Liam?
qa.a: They laughed warmly and Granny praised him for joining in, which makes the ritual feel like a place he belongs.

qa.q: How might Granny feel when Liam copies her prayer?
qa.a: She probably feels touched and happy to see him take part in the family practice.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler folding his hands and saying amen in imitation of family practice, expressing belonging rather than belief.
